opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and it's one I think about a lot. The way I see it, larger-scale models and cost-efficient models aren't really in tension. They're two parts of the same pipeline.

When we train very large models, like the work we did on PaLM, the goal is partly to push the frontier and see what capabilities emerge at scale. We saw things like multi-step reasoning, few-shot learning, and code generation get dramatically better as we scaled up. So the large model is the place where you find out what's possible at all.

But nobody wants to serve a model with hundreds of billions of parameters for every query if they don't have to. It's expensive, it's slow, and for many applications it's overkill. So the second step is asking how we take what the large model has learned and bring it into something smaller and cheaper to run. That's where distillation comes in, where the large model acts as a teacher, generating data or providing signals for a smaller student. Better data mixtures, better training recipes, and inference-time techniques like quantization and efficient attention help too.

There's also a third piece: the systems side. A lot of my background is in making training and inference efficient on hardware, things like how you partition a model across accelerators and how you keep utilization high. Even at large scale, you can get a lot more out of a fixed compute budget if the systems work is done well. That changes the cost curve for both the big models and the small ones.

So I'd say the large models are the engine of discovery and the source of supervision. The cost-efficient models are how those capabilities actually reach people. You really need both, and the interesting research question is how small you can go while keeping most of what makes the big model special.

r001.rationale: It says large models help reveal what capabilities are possible, but does not state that they reveal those capabilities sooner than smaller models.

r002.rationale: It explains that capabilities learned by a large model can be transferred to a smaller, cheaper student through distillation and suitable training.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a great question, and honestly it's something I think about constantly, because on the surface those two goals seem to be in tension. You've got this one camp saying scale is all you need, keep making the models bigger, and another camp saying we need models that are practical, that can actually run on a phone or serve millions of users without burning through a data center's worth of compute. I don't think of them as opposing camps. I think of large-scale models as the frontier that tells us what's possible, and then cost-efficient models as the engineering challenge of bringing that frontier to people.

When I was working on PaLM, one of the things that really struck me was how many capabilities just appeared as we scaled up. Things like multi-step reasoning, understanding jokes, explaining why something is funny. These weren't things we trained for explicitly. They emerged. And once you've seen that a capability exists at 540 billion parameters, you've essentially proven a point about what language models can do. That knowledge is incredibly valuable even if that particular model is too expensive to deploy broadly.

So the way I think about it is almost like a pipeline. The large model is the teacher, or the existence proof. It shows you the ceiling. Then the research question becomes, how much of that can I preserve as I bring the cost down? And there are a lot of levers there. Distillation, where you use the big model to generate training signal for a smaller one. Better data, because it turns out data quality buys you a lot of the gains that we used to attribute purely to parameter count. Architectural choices like mixture of experts, where you have a large total parameter count but only activate a fraction per token, so your inference cost looks like a much smaller model. And then the whole family of techniques around quantization and efficient serving.

What I find exciting right now is that the gap between the frontier model and the efficient model keeps closing faster than I expected. A model that's a tenth or a hundredth of the size can now do things that only the largest models could do a couple of years ago. Part of that is because we've learned so much from the big runs about what actually matters. The scaling work isn't wasted. It's informing where we spend the compute in the small model.

The other thing I'd say is that cost-efficiency isn't just about model size. It's about the whole system. How you serve the model, how you batch requests, whether you can cache things, whether you can route easy queries to a small model and only escalate the hard ones to the big one. When you think at the system level, the large model becomes one component rather than the whole answer, and that's really where I think the field is heading.

r001.rationale: It says capabilities emerged as the model scaled up, and that smaller models now do things that only the largest models could do earlier.

r002.rationale: It describes distillation, using a large model to generate training signal for a smaller one, and asks how much of the large model’s capabilities can be preserved as costs come down.

astra-6.text:
I think larger-scale models are a way to explore what capabilities are possible. As we scale, we can ask: Are we learning something that we couldn’t learn with a smaller model? And what is actually driving that improvement—is it the number of parameters, the amount of data, or the way we train the model?

But the largest model isn’t necessarily the model you want to deploy. Training cost matters, and so does the cost of serving that model repeatedly. So I think of capability and efficiency as connected goals. We want to understand what works at a larger scale, then use that understanding to make more efficient models—through better data, better training, or transferring capabilities to smaller models.

Ultimately, the question is what level of capability you need for a particular application, and how efficiently you can deliver it. Scale is one tool for getting there.

r001.rationale: The response says larger models help explore possible capabilities, but does not say they reveal capabilities sooner than smaller models.

r002.rationale: It says to learn what works at larger scale and then use that understanding to make efficient models, including by transferring capabilities to smaller models.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of larger-scale models as a way to explore what capabilities are possible and understand what drives them. But scale is one dimension. The question is how we balance model size, the amount and quality of training data, and the compute we spend to get the capabilities we need.

There’s also a distinction between the cost of training a model and the cost of serving it. If a model is going to be used many times, investing more in training a smaller model can make sense if it reduces inference cost while preserving quality. So I wouldn’t frame the goal as building the largest model. It’s about understanding those tradeoffs and finding an efficient model for the application.

r001.rationale: The response says larger models help explore possible capabilities, but does not state that they reveal them sooner than smaller models.

r002.rationale: The response discusses training smaller models for efficiency, but does not say that capabilities first found in large models can later be trained into smaller models.
